title: CI/CD shell steps
goal: Write the shell parts of a pipeline: retries with backoff, waiting for a port, version tags from git, a deploy with health check and rollback, and steps whose exit codes Jenkins and GitHub Actions understand.
setup: # P3: a small git repo with fixed dates, so commit ids are the same on every machine
rm -rf repo && git -c init.defaultBranch=main init -q repo
for msg in "first version" "add todo API" "fix login bug" "add health endpoint" "speed up list query"; do
unset GIT_AUTHOR_NAME GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL GIT_COMMITTER_NAME GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL G
# P4: releases for a symlink deploy, and a broken deploy script
for r in v1 v2-good v2-bad; do mkdir -p "releases/$r"; done

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Usage: deploy.sh RELEASE   (a folder in releases/, for example v2-good)' '# Switch "current" to the new release, check health, and roll back to the old release' '# if the check fails. The exit code must tell CI if the deploy worked.' 'NEW=$1' 'OLD=$(readlink current)' 'ln -sfn releases/$NEW current' 'if curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8141/current/health.json | grep -q UP; then' '  echo "deployed $NEW"' 'else' '  echo "health check failed, rolling back"' '  ln -sfn $NEW current' 'fi' > deploy.sh

warmup.q: How do you get the newest stable tag from a releases JSON API?
What is the safe pattern for an nginx config change?
warmup.a: Back up, put the new config in place, `nginx -t`, reload only if it passes, else restore.

warmup.q: Why do CI scripts need `set -o pipefail`?
warmup.a: Without it, `cmd | tee log` returns tee's exit code (0), so a failing `cmd` looks green.

warmup.q: How do you replace a symlink `current` in one step?

problems.title: retry with exponential backoff
problems.situation: The pipeline's `docker push` and `apt-get update` steps sometimes fail because of short network problems. Instead of failing the build, a `retry` function tries again, waiting 1, 2, 4 ... seconds (exponential backoff), up to a limit.
task: Write `retry MAX FIRST_DELAY command...`: run the command; on failure wait, double the delay, try again.
Print each failed try to stderr. After MAX tries, return 1.
Test with the given `flaky` function (works on the 3rd call).
Test with `false` and 2 tries: print the exit code.
hints: `shift 2` removes MAX and DELAY; then `"$@"` is the command.
`until "$@"; do ... done` loops while the command fails.
solution: retry() {      # usage: retry MAX_TRIES FIRST_DELAY command [args...]
if (( n >= max )); then echo "failed after $n tries: $*" >&2; return 1; fi
flaky() {      # fake network call: fails twice, then works

explanation.meaning: The rest of the arguments is the command, run exactly as given (Day 9).
Run the command; repeat the body while it fails (Day 8).
Exponential backoff: 1, 2, 4, 8 ... seconds. Gives a busy service time to recover.
A hard limit, so the pipeline fails clearly instead of hanging.
The caller (with `set -e`) stops the pipeline step.

mistakes: Retrying commands that are not safe to repeat (for example a database migration or a payment). Retry only idempotent steps.
Retrying a real error (wrong password, missing file) many times: it only makes the build slower. Retry network-type errors.
problems.interview_say: For flaky network steps I wrap the command in a retry function with a maximum number of tries and exponential backoff, and I only retry steps that are safe to run again.
problems.try_yourself: Add random jitter: `sleep $((delay + RANDOM % 2))`. Why does jitter help when many clients retry at the same time?

problems.title: wait_for_port before the next step
problems.situation: In the integration test stage, the pipeline starts PostgreSQL and the backend in containers, then runs tests at once, and the tests fail because the backend is not listening yet. A `wait_for_port` function waits until the port accepts connections, with a timeout.
task: Write `wait_for_port HOST PORT TIMEOUT` using bash's `/dev/tcp/HOST/PORT` (no extra tools).
Start a test server that begins listening after 2 seconds, in the background.
Wait for it (timeout 10). Then wait for a port that never opens (timeout 3) and print the exit code.
hints: `(echo > /dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/8142) 2>/dev/null` succeeds only if the port is open.
`nc -z HOST PORT` is another way, if netcat is installed.

explanation.meaning: A bash feature: opening this "file" makes a TCP connection. Works without nc or curl.
Try in a subshell and hide the `Connection refused` message.
Seconds waited so far.
The pipeline fails with a clear message instead of running tests against nothing.
A port can be open before the app is ready. For HTTP apps also wait for the health endpoint (Day 25).

problems.expected_output:
127.0.0.1:8142 is open
timeout: 127.0.0.1:8143 not open after 3s
exit code: 1
mistakes: `sleep 30` before the tests "to be safe": slow on good days, still too short on bad days. Wait for the real condition.
Using `/dev/tcp` in a script run by `sh`: it is a bash feature only.
problems.interview_say: Instead of fixed sleeps, my pipelines wait for the real condition: `wait_for_port` with `/dev/tcp` or `nc -z`, then the health endpoint, always with a timeout that fails the step.
problems.try_yourself: In Docker Compose, the same idea is a `healthcheck` plus `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`. Find one in a compose file you know.

problems.title: Version tags with git describe
problems.situation: Every build of the to-do backend needs a unique, readable version for the Docker tag and the release notes. `git describe` turns the last tag plus the commits since then into a version like `v1.2.0-3-g1a2b3c4`. The release job also needs the next patch version.
task: In `repo`, show the history with `git log --oneline --decorate` and the tags.
Run `git describe --tags` and explain the 3 parts.
Get only the last tag (`--abbrev=0`) and compute the next patch version (v1.2.0 → v1.2.1).
Change a file without committing, and run `git describe --tags --dirty`.
Build the Docker image name from the describe output.
hints: `v1.2.0-3-gXXXXXXX` = tag, commits since the tag, `g` + short commit id.
`IFS=. read -r MA MI PA <<< "${TAG#v}"` splits the numbers.
`--dirty` adds `-dirty` when there are uncommitted changes.

explanation.meaning: Nearest tag + number of commits since it + `g` + short commit id.
Only the tag name.
Split `1.2.0` at the dots into three variables (Day 4, Day 8).
Mark builds made from uncommitted code: they must never go to production.
Throw away the local change again.
Docker tags often drop the `v` (Day 13).

problems.expected_output:
f763ad2 (HEAD -> main) speed up list query
0c8bc65 add health endpoint
4a81894 fix login bug
59077f8 (tag: v1.2.0) add todo API
330c79d first version
v1.2.0
describe: v1.2.0-3-gf763ad2
last tag: v1.2.0, next patch: v1.2.1
with local changes: v1.2.0-3-gf763ad2-dirty
image: registry.example.com/todo-backend:1.2.0-3-gf763ad2
problems.output_note: Commit ids are the same as here because the setup used fixed names and dates.
mistakes: CI checks out with `--depth 1` (shallow clone): tags are missing and `git describe` fails with `fatal: No names found, cannot describe anything.` Fetch tags (`git fetch --tags --unshallow`) or use `--always`.
Using `latest` as the only tag: nobody can tell which code runs, and rolling back to a known version is hard.

checks.run: git init -q empty && cd empty && git describe --tags
checks.expect: fatal: No names found, cannot describe anything.

problems.interview_say: I version builds with `git describe --tags --always --dirty`: the last tag, commits since it, and the commit id. It is unique per commit, readable, and I can roll back to any version.
problems.try_yourself: Run `git describe --tags --always` in a folder with a new repo that has no tags. What does `--always` print?

problems.title: Find the bug: deploy with health check and rollback
problems.situation: `deploy.sh` switches the `current` symlink to a new release and checks its health. Yesterday a bad release stayed live after a failed check, CI showed the deploy as green, and a typo in the release name broke the site completely.
task: Start the test server: `python3 -m http.server 8141 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &`.
Run `bash deploy.sh v2-bad; echo $?` and then `readlink current`.
Reset with `ln -sfn releases/v1 current`. Run `bash deploy.sh v9; echo $?` (a release that does not exist).
Find 4 bugs: no check that the release exists, a health check that matches the wrong text, the rollback target, and the exit code.
Fix it and test `v2-bad`, `v9` and `v2-good`.
hints: `grep -q UP` also matches `UPGRADING_FAILED`. Match the exact JSON: `grep -q '"status": "UP"'`.
solution: bash deploy.sh v2-bad; echo "exit code: $?"; echo "current -> $(readlink current)"
bash deploy.sh v9; echo "exit code: $?"; echo "current -> $(readlink current)"
# Usage: deploy.sh RELEASE   (a folder in releases/, for example v2-good)
# Switch "current" to the new release, check health, and roll back to the old release
# if the check fails. The exit code must tell CI if the deploy worked.
[ -d "releases/$NEW" ] || { echo "error: release $NEW does not exist" >&2; exit 2; }
echo "health check failed, rolled back to $OLD" >&2
for r in v2-bad v9 v2-good; do
bash deploy.sh "$r"; echo "$r: exit code $?, current -> $(readlink current)"

explanation.meaning: Bug 1: `v9` created a broken symlink, so the site served nothing.
Bug 2: `grep -q UP` matched `UPGRADING_FAILED`.
Bug 3: the rollback pointed to `$NEW` (and even without `releases/`).
Bug 4: the script ended with 0, so CI showed a failed deploy as green.
Safe defaults (Day 22, Day 18).
`ln -sfn` changes the live release in one step, and rollback is the same command with the old target.

problems.expected_output:
deployed v2-bad
exit code: 0
current -> releases/v2-bad
health check failed, rolling back
exit code: 0
current -> v9
--- fixed ---
health check failed, rolled back to releases/v1
v2-bad: exit code 1, current -> releases/v1
error: release v9 does not exist
v9: exit code 2, current -> releases/v1
deployed v2-good
v2-good: exit code 0, current -> releases/v2-good
mistakes: Checking health only once, at once after the switch: some apps need a few seconds. Use the retry function from P1.
Rolling back without an alert: the team does not know the release failed. Exit non-zero so CI reports it.
problems.interview_say: My deploy script validates the input, switches the release with an atomic symlink, runs a health check with timeout, and on failure rolls back to the previous release and exits non-zero so the pipeline goes red.
problems.try_yourself: Use `retry 3 1 check_health` from P1 instead of a single check.

problems.title: Pipeline steps: exit codes for Jenkins and GitHub Actions
problems.situation: Jenkins `sh` steps and GitHub Actions `run:` steps are bash scripts: a non-zero exit code fails the stage. The user writes a small parameterised runner `ci.sh --env ENV --steps a,b,c [--dry-run]` that runs steps in order, stops at the first failure, and prints a GitHub Actions error annotation.
task: Parse long options with a `while`/`case`/`shift` loop: `--env`, `--steps`, `--dry-run`. Validate `--env`.
Split `--steps` at commas into an array.
Run `steps/NAME.sh` for each step; on failure print `::error::step NAME failed (exit N)` and exit with that code.
Run it: dry run for all steps; real run for `lint,test,deploy`; real run for `lint,deploy`.
hints: `while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do case $1 in --env) ENV=$2; shift 2 ;; ... esac; done`
solution: usage() { echo "usage: ci.sh --env dev|staging|prod --steps a,b,c [--dry-run]" >&2; exit 2; }
if $DRY; then echo "[dry-run] would run steps/$s.sh for $ENV"; continue; fi
bash "steps/$s.sh" || { rc=$?; echo "::endgroup::"; echo "::error::step $s failed (exit $rc)"; exit $rc; }
bash ci.sh --env staging --steps lint,test,deploy --dry-run; echo "exit code: $?"
bash ci.sh --env staging --steps lint,test,deploy; echo "exit code: $?"
bash ci.sh --env staging --steps lint,deploy; echo "exit code: $?"
bash ci.sh --env qa --steps lint; echo "exit code: $?"

explanation.meaning: Parse long options (`--env value`); getopts only knows short ones (Day 9).
Split a comma list into an array.
Keep the original exit code of the failed step and stop.
GitHub Actions workflow commands: fold the log, and show a red annotation. Jenkins just shows the text.
`sh './ci.sh --env staging --steps lint,test'` — a non-zero exit fails the stage.
`run: ./ci.sh --env staging --steps lint,test` — the runner uses `bash -e`, and non-zero fails the job.

problems.expected_output:
[dry-run] would run steps/lint.sh for staging
[dry-run] would run steps/test.sh for staging
[dry-run] would run steps/deploy.sh for staging
pipeline OK for staging
exit code: 0
---
::group::lint
lint: 0 problems
::endgroup::
::group::test
test: 41 passed, 1 failed
::endgroup::
::error::step test failed (exit 1)
exit code: 1
---
::group::lint
lint: 0 problems
::endgroup::
::group::deploy
deploy: done
::endgroup::
pipeline OK for staging
exit code: 0
usage: ci.sh --env dev|staging|prod --steps a,b,c [--dry-run]
exit code: 2
mistakes: `|| echo "failed"` without `exit`: the step prints an error but the pipeline continues and deploys untested code.
Different behavior on CI and laptops because of `sh` vs `bash`. Put `#!/bin/bash` and call scripts with `bash`, or set `shell: bash` in GitHub Actions.
problems.interview_say: In Jenkins and GitHub Actions every shell step passes or fails by its exit code. My CI scripts use `set -euo pipefail`, take parameters as options, stop at the first failing step, and keep that step's exit code.
problems.try_yourself: Add `--retries N` and run each step with `retry N 1 bash steps/$s.sh` from P1.

problems.title: Compare versions with sort -V (no downgrades)
problems.situation: A deploy pipeline must refuse to deploy an older version by mistake (for example `v1.9.2` over `v1.10.0`). Text sorting puts `v1.10.0` before `v1.9.2`; version sorting with `sort -V` gets it right.
task: Sort `v1.9.2 v1.10.0 v1.2.0` with `sort` and with `sort -V`. Compare.
Write `is_newer A B` that is true when A is newer than B.
hints: A is newer if it is the last one and not equal to B.
solution: printf '%s\n' v1.9.2 v1.10.0 v1.2.0 | sort | xargs echo "text sort:   "
printf '%s\n' v1.9.2 v1.10.0 v1.2.0 | sort -V | xargs echo "version sort:"
is_newer v1.10.0 v1.9.2 && echo "v1.10.0 is newer than v1.9.2: deploy"
is_newer v1.2.0 v1.10.0 || echo "v1.2.0 is not newer than v1.10.0: refuse (downgrade)"

explanation.meaning: Text order compares character by character: `1` < `9`, so `v1.10` comes first.
Version order: numbers inside the text are compared as numbers.
Returns 0 (true) or 1 (false), so it works in `if` and with `&&`/`||` (Day 9).

problems.expected_output:
text sort:    v1.10.0 v1.2.0 v1.9.2
version sort: v1.2.0 v1.9.2 v1.10.0
v1.10.0 is newer than v1.9.2: deploy
v1.2.0 is not newer than v1.10.0: refuse (downgrade)
mistakes: Comparing versions as strings with `[[ $a > $b ]]`: `v1.10.0` is "smaller" than `v1.9.2` in text order.
problems.interview_say: To compare versions in bash I use `sort -V`, which sorts numbers inside the version as numbers. That lets a pipeline refuse accidental downgrades.
problems.try_yourself: Where does `v1.10.0-rc1` go in `sort -V` compared to `v1.10.0`? Is that what you want for pre-releases?

interview.q: How do Jenkins and GitHub Actions know if a shell step failed?
interview.a: Only by the exit code: 0 passes, anything else fails the step. That is why CI scripts need `set -euo pipefail` and must not hide errors.

interview.q: How would you write a retry for a flaky command?
interview.a: A loop with a maximum number of tries and a growing sleep (exponential backoff), running `"$@"` and returning non-zero after the last failure.

interview.q: How do you wait for a service in a pipeline?
interview.a: Wait for the real condition with a timeout: `wait_for_port` (`/dev/tcp` or `nc -z`) and then the health endpoint with `curl -f`. Not a fixed `sleep`.

interview.q: How do you create a version for every build?
interview.a: `git describe --tags --always --dirty` gives the last tag, commits since it and the commit id, for example `v1.2.0-3-g1a2b3c4`.

interview.q: How does a deploy script roll back?
interview.a: Keep the previous release, switch to the new one, check health; if it fails, switch back (for example `ln -sfn` to the old release or `kubectl rollout undo`) and exit non-zero.

recap.meaning: Test a TCP port with bash only
